{{Short description|American physicist and academic (1938–2024)}}
'''Howard J. Van Till''' (November 28, 1938 – July 31, 2024) was an American physicist and emeritus professor of physics at [[Calvin College]], where he taught for 31 years. His research included [[solid state physics]] and [[millimeter-wave astronomy]]. He is also noted as a writer on science and Christianity.<ref name=CFI/>

==Early life==
Van Till was born in 1938 and grew up on a farm in California. When he was a child, he took a bottle of turkey medication from his parents' farm, mixed it with some mineral powders, and shook it; this resulted in the bottle exploding, causing him to lose a considerable amount of blood from his [[jugular vein]].<ref name=GRP>{{cite web | url=http://blog.mlive.com/grpress/2008/02/scientist_still_explores_myste.html | title=Scientist still explores 'mystery' of God | work=[[Grand Rapids Press]] | date=2 February 2008 | accessdate=21 January 2014 | author=Honey, Charley}}</ref>

==Religious views==
Van Till was brought up as a [[Calvinist]], and known for such beliefs for much of his life. He has been active in writing and speaking on the interaction of science and Christian belief, for example as a member of the editorial boards of ''[[Science and Christian Belief]]'' and ''[[Theology and Science]]'', and working with the [[Templeton Foundation]].<ref name=CFI/>

In 2006 he gave a presentation to the [[Freethought]] Association of West Michigan in which he recounted that he had less certainty than before on some religious questions.<ref name=CFI>{{cite web|title=From Calvinism to Freethought: The Road Less Traveled|url=http://www.cfimichigan.org/pastevents/event/from-calvinism-to-freethought-the-road-less-traveled/|work=Presentation by Howard Van Till|publisher=[[Center for Inquiry]]|accessdate=January 26, 2014|author=Charles LaRue|location=Michigan|date=May 24, 2006}}</ref><ref>[http://www.freethoughtassociation.org/images/uploads/pdf/ODoRs.pdf ''From Calvinism to Freethought'']</ref>
He now attends a more liberal church.<ref name=GRP/>

===Opposition to creationism===
In 1986 Van Till published ''The Fourth Day'', which sought to reconcile Christianity with Darwinist science. Writing in 2006, [[Russell D. Moore]] described this work as "monumental", and Van Till as "the most lauded and prolific defender of theistic evolution among American evangelicals".<ref>{{cite web|title=A Theistic Evolutionist Turns Off the Light|url=http://www.russellmoore.com/2006/07/26/a-theistic-evolutionist-turns-off-the-light/|accessdate=January 26, 2014|author=Russell D. Moore|authorlink=Russell D. Moore|date=July 26, 2006}}</ref>

In 1988 Van Till co-wrote ''Science Held Hostage: What's wrong with creation science and evolution'' with [[Davis A. Young]] and [[Clarence Menninga]].<ref name=numbers>[[Ronald L. Numbers]]. ''Darwinism comes to America''. [[Harvard University Press]], 1998. {{ISBN|0-674-19312-1}} pp.12,57,163,</ref>

He was publicly accused of [[heresy]] after the issue of ''The Fourth Day'',<ref name=GRP/> and Van Till's professorship was subject for four years to a monthly review of his beliefs and eligibility to teach at Calvin College. He continued to teach until 1999, but his Calvinist faith was affected by the inquiry.<ref>{{cite news|author=Jeremy Manier| title=The New Theology| url=https://www.chicagotribune.com/2008/01/20/the-new-theology/ |access-date=February 16, 2014| newspaper=Chicago Tribune| date=January 20, 2008}}</ref>

An article of his in 1996, claiming that theistic evolution was compatible with the teaching of renowned church fathers [[Augustine of Hippo|Augustine]] and [[Basil of Caesarea|Basil]],<ref>[http://www.asa3.org/ASA/topics/evolution/S&CB4-96VanTill.html Basil, Augustine, and the Doctrine of Creation’s Functional Integrity] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090126095505/http://www.asa3.org/ASA/topics/evolution/S%26CB4-96VanTill.html |date=2009-01-26 }}, ''Science & Christian Belief'' 8, No. 1 (1996): 21-38.</ref> drew rebuttals from [[Jonathan Wells (intelligent design advocate)|Jonathan Wells]]<ref>[http://www.arn.org/docs/odesign/od191/abusingtheology191.htm Abusing Theology: Howard Van Till's "Forgotten Doctrine of Creation's Functional Integrity"],  [[Jonathan Wells (intelligent design advocate)|Jonathan Wells]], [[Discovery Institute]], 1998. Retrieved February 16, 2014.</ref> and John Mark Reynolds,<ref>[http://www.arn.org/docs/odesign/od191/gaplesseconomy191.htm Are There Gaps in the Gapless Economy? The Improbable Views of Howard J. Van Till], John Mark Reynolds, Director, [[Torrey Honors Institute]], Biola University, 1998. Retrieved February 16, 2014.</ref> to which Van Till responded in turn.<ref>{{cite web|last=Van Till|title=Basil and Augustine Revisited: The Survival of Functional Integrity|url=http://www.arn.org/docs/odesign/od191/basilaug191.htm|work=[[Origins and Design]]|publisher=Access Research Network|accessdate=February 16, 2014|year=1998}}</ref>

[[Ronald L. Numbers]] in 1998 stated that Van Till is a devout Christian who sees little or no evidence of God in nature and whose view is a good example of "[[theistic evolution]]". However, Numbers records that Van Till prefers the term "creationomic perspective" over "theistic evolution".<ref name="numbers" />

In a February 2016 article in ''Theology and Science'': "SOBIG; A Symposium on Belief in God",<ref>{{cite journal|doi=10.1080/14746700.2015.1122323|journal=Theology and Science|volume =14|year= 2016 | issue =1|title=SOBIG: A Symposium on Belief in God | author = Howard J. Van Till|pages =6–35}}</ref> he now describes his theological and philosophical view as "a comprehensive but non-reductive naturalism".

Van Till died on July 31, 2024, at the age of 85.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Howard Van Till Obituary (1938 - 2024) - Grand Rapids, MI - Grand Rapids Press |url=https://obits.mlive.com/us/obituaries/grandrapids/name/howard-van-till-obituary?id=55743108 |access-date=2024-11-06 |website=Legacy.com}}</ref>
